hints: Think about the charge on the metal or non-metal ion combined with $\text{O}^{2-}$ to work out the formula of each oxide first.
Balance oxygen last by checking atoms on both sides, remembering oxygen is $\text{O}_2$ as a reactant.
walkthrough:
Work out the product formula for sodium oxide**
Sodium is Group 1 so forms $\text{Na}^{+}$, oxygen forms $\text{O}^{2-}$. To balance charges you need two $\text{Na}^{+}$ for each $\text{O}^{2-}$, giving $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$. Then balance: $4\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}$.

Work out the product formula for sulfur oxide**
Sulfur burning in oxygen under normal conditions gives sulfur dioxide, $\text{SO}_2$. The atoms already balance with one $\text{O}_2$ molecule: $\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$.

Final answer: $4\text{Na} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_2\text{O}$
$\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$

hints: Decide what ions are present in $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and remember aluminium loses all three outer electrons.
walkthrough:
Picture the electron transfer**
Aluminium is $2,8,3$ so each Al loses 3 electrons to form $\text{Al}^{3+}$ with an empty outer shell, so you draw just $\text{Al}^{3+}$ with no dots or crosses around it. Oxygen is $2,6$ so each O gains 2 electrons to form $\text{O}^{2-}$ with a full octet.
Step 2: **Show the correct ratio and octet**
You need two $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ions and three $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions for $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$. Around each $\text{O}^{2-}$ draw 8 electrons, using e.g. crosses for the original O electrons and dots for the electrons gained from Al.
Final answer: Show $2 \times \text{Al}^{3+}$ with no outer electrons and $3 \times \text{O}^{2-}$ each surrounded by 8 outer electrons (mixture of dots and crosses).

hints: List the formulae of the highest oxides across Period 3 from $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ to $\text{SO}_3$ and work out the oxidation number of the Period 3 element in each.
Link that oxidation number to the Group number and the number of outer shell electrons the atom can lose or share.
walkthrough:
Spot the pattern in numbers**
In $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ Na is +1, in MgO Mg is +2, in $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ Al is +3, in $\text{SiO}_2$ Si is +4, in $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ P is +5, in $\text{SO}_3$ S is +6. So the maximum oxidation state climbs steadily from +1 to +7 (for Cl).

Explain with electrons**
Moving across Period 3 you add one proton and one valence electron at a time. That extra valence electron is available to be lost to form ions or shared to form covalent bonds with oxygen, so the element can reach a higher positive oxidation state.

Final answer: Maximum oxidation state increases across the period.
This is because the number of valence electrons that can be lost or shared in bonding increases across the period.

hints: Recall whether MgO is metallic basic and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is non-metallic acidic, and what type of solution each forms with water.
Remember MgO is only sparingly soluble giving a weakly alkaline solution, while $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ gives a strong acid.
walkthrough:
Complete the magnesium row**
$\text{MgO}$ is a basic oxide. With water: $\text{MgO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2$. The hydroxide is only slightly soluble so you get a weakly alkaline solution, pH around 9 to 10.

Complete the phosphorus row**
$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ is an acidic oxide. With water: $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. Phosphoric acid is acidic so pH is low, around 1 to 2.

Final answer: Row 1: Period 3 oxide $\text{MgO}$, product $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, pH approx 9 to 10 (any value $8 \leqslant \text{pH} \leqslant 12$).
Row 2: Period 3 oxide $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, product $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, pH approx 1 to 2 (any value $1 \leqslant \text{pH} \leqslant 4$).

hints: Remember acid hydrolysis of a nitrile $\text{R-CN}$ breaks the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bond to give a carboxylic acid plus an ammonium ion.
walkthrough:
Build the hydrolysis products**
The $-\text{CN}$ carbon becomes the $-\text{COOH}$ carbon, so $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$ gives $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. The nitrogen ends up as $\text{NH}_4^{+}$ in acid. To balance O and H you need $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $1\text{H}^{+}$ on the left: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^{+}$.

hints: Draw propene $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ and see that adding $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ across the double bond can happen two ways.
Place the $\text{OH}$ on the middle carbon for one isomer and on the end carbon for the other isomer.
walkthrough:
Add OH to the middle carbon**
If $\text{H}$ adds to the end $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{OH}$ adds to the middle $\text{CH}$, you get the major product propan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_3$, a secondary alcohol.

Add OH to the end carbon**
If the addition happens the opposite way round, $\text{OH}$ ends up on the terminal carbon to give the minor product propan-1-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$, a primary alcohol. Draw both with all bonds shown clearly.

Final answer: Propan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$
Propan-1-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (displayed or skeletal structures accepted).

hints: Compare $\text{R-O-H}$ with $\text{H-O-H}$ and think about how an alkyl group R pushes electrons compared with H.
Think about how extra electron density on oxygen affects the ease of breaking the $\text{O-H}$ bond to release $\text{H}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
See the inductive push**
In water the groups attached to O are just H atoms. In an alcohol one H is replaced by an alkyl group, which pushes electrons towards the oxygen. We call this an electron donating or positive inductive effect.

Link to acidity**
Acidity means losing $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{O-H}$. Extra electron density on O makes the $\text{O-H}$ bond stronger and less polar in the sense of releasing $\text{H}^{+}$, and it also destabilises the $\text{RO}^{-}$ anion formed. So the equilibrium $\text{ROH} \rightleftharpoons \text{RO}^{-} + \text{H}^{+}$ lies further to the left than for water.

Final answer: Alkyl groups are electron donating (positive inductive effect).
This increases electron density on oxygen, strengthens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and makes release of $\text{H}^{+}$ less favourable.

hints: Read the bar heights for $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ from Fig. 2.1 and state the direction of the trend.
Think about what changes down Group 16 in terms of molecular size and total electrons, and which intermolecular force depends on this.
walkthrough:
Describe the trend**
Fig. 2.1 shows boiling point rising from $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (about 213 K) to $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$. These are all simple molecular hydrides with no hydrogen bonding, so the only forces to overcome are London dispersion forces.

Explain with electrons**
Going down the group S to Se to Te, each molecule has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud. This creates larger temporary dipoles and therefore stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces. More thermal energy is required to break these attractions, so boiling point increases.

Final answer: Boiling point increases from $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ as the molecules have a greater number of electrons.
This gives stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London dispersion) forces, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

hints: Check which of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ can form hydrogen bonds by looking at the electronegativity and size of O versus S.
walkthrough:
Spot the extra force in water**
Oxygen is small and very electronegative, so $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ can form strong hydrogen bonds between molecules. Sulfur is larger and less electronegative, so $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ cannot form hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bonds need far more energy to break than London forces, which is why water boils at about 373 K, far above $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.

Final answer: Only $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has hydrogen bonding, which is much stronger than the London dispersion / permanent dipole-dipole forces in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, so much more energy is needed to separate $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules.
